szoveg_eredeti:
Neurosurgical Artificial Intelligence Models Face Critical Validation and Calibration Limitations Across Subspecialties

A comprehensive systematic review evaluating five years of predictive artificial intelligence research in neurosurgery has revealed that while computational models demonstrate consistently high discriminative accuracy, pervasive deficiencies in statistical calibration and external validation continue to hinder safe clinical translation. Predictive modeling using artificial intelligence has expanded rapidly across surgical subdisciplines, supported by the convergence of large electronic health record datasets, advanced neuroimaging pipelines, and maturing machine learning architectures. These computational systems are intended to support complex neurosurgical practice by improving preoperative risk stratification, patient-specific outcome forecasting, surgical planning, and clinical decision-making. However, a rigorous assessment of the published literature indicates that the technical sophistication of an algorithm does not guarantee clinical reliability, as models frequently suffer from significant performance degradation when applied to independent patient populations and routinely omit evaluations of probability agreement.

The systematic review was conducted in full compliance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and was formally registered in the PROSPERO database under registration number CRD420261373632. Researchers Zeynab Alizada, Aida Gafarova, Rauf Nasirov, Edin Nevzati, Antiga Muradova, and Natig Ahmadov established a structured PICOTS framework to examine peer-reviewed studies published between March 1, 2021, and March 31, 2026. The investigative team searched PubMed/MEDLINE and the Web of Science Core Collection using a structured two-block Boolean search strategy combining controlled MeSH terms and free-text keywords spanning neurosurgical diseases and procedures alongside artificial intelligence and machine learning methodologies. Databases such as Embase and IEEE Xplore were omitted from the primary search, with the authors noting that IEEE Xplore predominantly indexes engineering and computer science conference proceedings lacking the human patient-level clinical endpoints required by the review criteria. Hand-searching of reference lists supplemented the database queries to capture all relevant investigations.

Methodological quality across the primary prediction studies was formally evaluated using the Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool, known as PROBAST, which evaluates potential bias across four distinct domains: participants, predictors, outcome, and statistical analysis. Reporting quality was assessed using the Transparent Reporting of a Multivariable Prediction Model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis checklist, commonly designated as TRIPOD, alongside supplementary evaluation criteria adapted for benchmark evaluations of large language models. The systematic screening protocol yielded 29 eligible publications meeting all predefined inclusion criteria. This corpus comprised 23 primary predictive model studies, two benchmark evaluations analyzing large language models on standardized neurosurgical examinations, and four systematic reviews or dedicated methodological quality appraisals. The temporal trajectory of publications showed marked expansion over the five-year period, rising from two papers in 2021 and five in 2022 to a peak of 10 in 2023, followed by six in 2024, five in 2025, and one in early 2026.

Among the 23 primary predictive model studies, computational investigations were distributed across six clinical subspecialties. Neuro-oncology and cerebrovascular neurosurgery represented the co-dominant areas of investigation, each accounting for six publications, or 26.1 percent of the primary evidence base. Spine surgery represented four studies, comprising 17.4 percent, while traumatic brain injury accounted for three studies, or 13.0 percent. The remaining four investigations were split equally between epilepsy or functional neurosurgery and pediatric neurosurgery focusing on hydrocephalus, each representing two studies, or 8.7 percent. General supervised machine learning algorithms constituted the dominant computational category across the primary literature, appearing in 16 of the 23 studies, or 69.6 percent. Combined machine learning and radiomics pipelines accounted for two studies, end-to-end deep learning architectures appeared in two studies, while hybrid deep learning and machine learning, explainable machine learning utilizing SHapley Additive exPlanations, and algorithmic complexity comparisons each represented single studies.

Across all 23 primary studies reporting numerical discrimination metrics, model performance appeared ostensibly robust. Every primary study reported an extractable area under the receiver operating characteristic curve or concordance statistic, yielding a range of 0.672 to 0.940, with a median of 0.827, a mean of 0.818, and a standard deviation of 0.092. The highest reported discrimination value in the review occurred in a spine surgery study by Santipas and colleagues evaluating cervical spine metastasis, which reported an area under the curve of 0.940 using gradient boosting; however, this estimate was derived from a small cohort of only 72 patients, severely limiting its statistical generalizability. Similarly, in neurovascular applications, Turhon and colleagues reported an internal area under the curve of 0.929 using deep learning on multi-omics computed tomography angiography data from 1,809 aneurysms across two institutions, which moderated to external discrimination values between 0.823 and 0.876.

Despite these favorable discrimination metrics, formal risk of bias evaluations using PROBAST revealed profound methodological vulnerabilities across the primary predictive literature. Only one study among the 23 primary reports, representing just 4.3 percent, was classified as having a low risk of bias. Nine studies, or 39.1 percent, demonstrated low-to-moderate risk, while 10 studies, representing 43.5 percent, exhibited high risk of bias, and three studies, or 13.0 percent, were categorized as having unclear risk. High or unclear risk classifications were predominantly driven by absent external validation, complete omission of calibration assessments, small overall sample sizes with inadequate event counts, and incomplete reporting of missing data handling. The solitary primary study achieving a low risk of bias rating was conducted by Fujimura and colleagues, published in JAMA Network Open, which developed and formally calibrated a Light Gradient Boosting Machine model to predict two-year unruptured intracranial aneurysm rupture risk across four medical centers located in Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States, outperforming established clinical scores including PHASES and UCAS.

The review identified a critical deficit in statistical calibration as one of the most pressing patient safety concerns facing neurosurgical artificial intelligence. Calibration measures the concordance between predicted probabilities generated by a mathematical model and the actual observed frequencies of clinical events. While a model can achieve a high discriminative area under the curve by correctly ranking patients relative to one another, poor calibration means it can systematically assign inaccurate absolute risk percentages to individual patients, such as assigning a 70 percent risk to individuals with a true event likelihood of 20 percent. Despite its clinical importance, formal calibration was documented in only six of the 23 primary studies, representing an overall reporting rate of just 26.1 percent.
